chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ribab, from Abu Ubaydah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), in [a narration]:

In the case of a man who married a woman from her guardian, and then found a defect in her after he had consummated the marriage with her, he said: If the blind woman concealed her blindness, the leper concealed his leprosy, the insane woman concealed her insanity, the woman with exposed private parts concealed it, and anyone who had an obvious defect concealed it, then she is returned to her family without divorce, and the husband takes the dowry from the guardian who concealed it. If the guardian was not aware of anything of that, then he has nothing against him, and she is returned to her family. He said: If the husband suffered a loss from what she took from him, it is for him; and if he did not suffer a loss, then he has nothing. He said: She observes a waiting period from him as a divorced woman if he had consummated the marriage with her; and if he had not consummated the marriage with her, then there is no waiting period upon her and she has no dowry.

The way to reconcile between these narrations is that what is added to insanity, leprosy, leprosy (white spots), blindness, and exposure of private parts, such as blindness, lameness, and obvious defects, which some narrations include, are held to be of a type of mild dislike (karahah), and it is recommended for one who is tested with that not to return her. As for the five things we mentioned, he has the right to return her in all cases, and that which confirms what we said is...

key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَة: Mild dislike or recommendation to avoid, short of prohibition
key_terms.الْمُفْضَاةُ: The woman with exposed private parts
key_terms.عَيْب: Defect or flaw in a person or object

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for returning a wife if a defect was concealed before marriage?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Baqir (AS), establishing a jurisprudential distinction between five specific major defects (insanity, leprosy, blindness, impotence, and obvious chronic illness) that warrant annulment without divorce, and other minor defects which are merely recommended to be overlooked. The text clarifies that if the wali (guardian) concealed the defect knowingly, the husband retains the full dowry; otherwise, he receives no compensation, reflecting the Shia principle of 'gharar' (uncertainty) in marriage contracts. This hadith serves as a foundational text for the doctrine of 'khiyar al-ayb' (option of defect) in Shia fiqh, emphasizing the guardian's duty of disclosure.
